# Book I, Proposition 10

*A given finite straight line, bisected*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> To bisect a given finite straight line.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved, as Euclid states it · Euclid's argument

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/10-idea.svg" alt="Stand a triangle with equal sides (blue) on the straight line and split its top angle into two equal parts (yellow): the dividing line cuts the base in half (red)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Stand a triangle with equal sides (blue) on the straight line and split its top angle into two equal parts (yellow): the dividing line cuts the base in half (red).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/10.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.10, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let AB be the given finite straight line.

Thus it is required to bisect the finite straight line AB.

Let the equilateral triangle ABC be constructed on it, [I. 1]

and let the angle ACB be bisected by the straight line CD; [I. 9]

I say that the straight line AB has been bisected at the point D.

For, since AC is equal to CB,

and CD is common,

the two sides AC, CD are equal to the two sides BC, CD respectively;

and the angle ACD is equal to the angle BCD;

therefore the base AD is equal to the base BD. [I. 4]

Therefore the given finite straight line AB has been bisected at D.

Q. E. F.

Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where a lemma does a step Euclid takes for granted; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Done by `crossbar`.** "and let the angle ACB be bisected by the straight line CD…" Euclid takes D to lie on AB between A and B. After I.9 gives a bisector within the angle ACB, `crossbar` finds its meeting D with AB on the ray from C through I.9's point F; the Lean then uses `angle_onRay_right` and `angle_onRay_left`, with angle symmetry, to identify ACD and BCD with the angles ACF and FCB that I.9 made equal.

```lean
/-- To bisect a given finite straight line. -/
theorem Prop10 {A B : Point} (hAB : A ≠ B) :
    ∃ D : Point, Between A D B ∧ ‖A D‖ = ‖D B‖ := by
  -- Let AB be the given finite straight line.
  /- Our proof names the straight line itself, to say later that D is on it
     and C is off it. -/
  obtain ⟨L, hA_L, hB_L⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  -- Thus it is required to bisect the finite straight line AB.
  -- Let the equilateral triangle ABC be constructed on it, [I. 1]
  /- No side of AB matters here, so I.1 is given a point of AB itself, A,
     as the point whose side the triangle is to be on. -/
  obtain ⟨C, ⟨hABC, -, hBC_CA⟩, -⟩ := Prop1 A B hAB A
  have hC_L : ¬ OnLine C L := hABC.off_line hA_L hB_L
  -- and let the angle ACB be bisected by the straight line CD; [I. 9]
  /- I.9 bisects the angle ACB by a straight line CF, with F within the
     angle: on B's side of CA and on A's side of CB. Euclid's D is the
     point where that straight line meets AB. He draws it there without a
     word; it is the crossbar (Book Zero, `crossbar`) that makes the bisector,
     falling within the angle, cross the base between A and B. -/
  obtain ⟨F, hF_CA, hF_CB, hACF_FCB, -⟩ := Prop9 hABC.acb
  obtain ⟨D, hADB, hD_CF⟩ := crossbar hF_CA hF_CB
  have hD_L : OnLine D L := on_line_of_between_ends hADB hA_L hB_L
  have hDC : D ≠ C := hD_CF.2.1
  -- I say that the straight line AB has been bisected at the point D.
  -- For, since AC is equal to CB,
  have hAC_CB : ‖A C‖ = ‖C B‖ :=
    (len_symm A C).trans (hBC_CA.symm.trans (len_symm B C))
  -- and CD is common,
  have hCD : ‖C D‖ = ‖C D‖ := rfl
  -- the two sides AC, CD are equal to the two sides BC, CD respectively;
  have hCA_CB : ‖C A‖ = ‖C B‖ := (len_symm C A).trans hAC_CB
  -- and the angle ACD is equal to the angle BCD;
  /- The angles ACD and BCD are the halves ACF and FCB that I.9 made equal,
     since D is on the ray from C through F (`angle_onRay_right`,
     `angle_onRay_left`); the second is then read the other way round. -/
  have hACD_BCD : ∠ A C D = ∠ B C D := by
    rw [angle_onRay_right hD_CF hABC.ne₁₃, hACF_FCB,
      ← angle_onRay_left hD_CF hABC.ne₂₃, angle_symm hDC hABC.ne₂₃]
  -- therefore the base AD is equal to the base BD. [I. 4]
  /- The two triangles are CAD and CBD: D is on AB, and C is off it. -/
  have hCAD : Triangle C A D := (Triangle.of_line hA_L hD_L (ne_of_between hADB) hC_L).cab
  have hCBD : Triangle C B D :=
    (Triangle.of_line hB_L hD_L (ne_of_between (between_symm hADB)) hC_L).cab
  have hAD_BD : ‖A D‖ = ‖B D‖ := (Prop4 hCAD hCBD hCA_CB hCD hACD_BCD).1
  -- Therefore the given finite straight line AB has been bisected at D.
  exact ⟨D, hADB, hAD_BD.trans (len_symm B D)⟩
  -- Q. E. F.
```

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L65): If B is between A and C, and D is between A and B, then D is between A and C. (Between 4)
- [`between_of_between_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L69): If B is between A and C, and C is between B and D, then B is between A and D. (Between 5)

If C lies within the angle BAD (on D's side of L and on B's side of N), then B and D are not on the same side of M: the straight line AC separates them. (Triple incidence 1)

**Superposition**

- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

Euclid bisects the angle ACB by the straight line CD and at once treats D as a point of AB, between A and B. Our I.9 hands back a bisector that falls within the angle, for just this use, and [Book Zero](../../Elements/Figure)'s [`crossbar`](../../Elements/Figure/Angles.lean), the crossbar theorem of the geometry books that follow David Hilbert, finds D: the bisector's straight line separates A from B, so it crosses AB, and Pasch's rules put the crossing between them, on the ray from C along the bisector. The rest of the proof is Euclid's.

Apollonius, Proclus reports, "bisected a straight line AB by a construction like that of I. 1" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 268): two circles about A and B with radius AB meet at C and D, and CD, joined, bisects the angle ACB by I.8 and then AB by I.4. It is the construction taught with ruler and compass today. Heath's complaint is one of method. Instead of assuming the bisection of the angle, done already in I.9, Apollonius "unnecessarily does over again what has been done before, which is open to objection from a theoretical point of view" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 268). We take Euclid's way, and cite I.9; under I.11 Heath finds a kinder word for Apollonius.

Can every line be halved? Proclus "warns us against being moved by this proposition to conclude that geometers assumed, as a preliminary hypothesis, that a line is not made up of indivisible parts" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 268), for a line of an odd number of indivisibles could not be halved at all. Following Geminus, Proclus answers that geometers assumed only that a continuous magnitude is divisible. "But *infinite* divisibility was not assumed by them" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 268): they proved it, in showing that some magnitudes are incommensurable. He adds that I.10 may serve to refute the indivisible lines of Xenocrates. Our I.10 assumes nothing of the kind: its D is simply where two straight lines cross.

## Further reading

- The crossbar theorem that finds D, and Pasch's axiom behind it, are in ch. 3, "Hilbert's Axioms", of Marvin Jay Greenberg's [*Euclidean and Non-Euclidean Geometries*](https://store.macmillanlearning.com/us/product/Euclidean-and-Non-Euclidean-Geometries/p/0716799480) (2008), a friendly textbook on the rules of order that Euclid leaves unsaid.
- Why do those rules of "between" matter? In Felix Klein's [*Elementary Mathematics from a Higher Standpoint, Volume II: Geometry*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-49445-5) (2016), Gert Schubring's translation of his lectures of 1908, the section on the *Elements* points out that Euclid has no axioms of betweenness, the gap through which the old geometric sophisms slip.
